our_prose: Harvest acorn squash once at full maturity, not young. The reliable ripeness sign is the ground spot, the patch where the fruit rests on the soil, which turns from cream or yellow to a deep orange; the rind should also be hard enough that a thumbnail cannot dent it, dull rather than glossy, and the stem dried and corky. Do not go by the dark green rind alone, since acorn squash colors up weeks before it is ripe. Cut the fruit from the vine with shears or a knife, leaving a 1 to 2 inch handle of stem, and avoid carrying it by the stem. Get the crop in before a hard frost, which damages the rind and shortens storage. Acorn squash is good to eat straight from the vine and, unlike a butternut, should not be cured: the heat and humidity of curing reduce its quality and shorten its already brief storage.

our_prose: This is the most important thing about growing apples: one apple tree on its own usually will not make fruit. Apple flowers need pollen from a different apple variety, carried over by bees. So plan to plant two different kinds of apple, not two of the same, within about 50 ft of each other, and make sure they bloom at the same time (an early bloomer cannot help a late bloomer). If you only have room for the idea of one tree, a flowering crabapple planted nearby can do the pollinating job instead. Golden Delicious is a reliable all-around partner that pollinates almost any apple. A few special varieties (Mutsu, Jonagold, Shizuka) cannot pollinate anything and actually need two other partners themselves, so ask the nursery if a variety is "triploid" before you rely on it as your second tree.

our_prose: Both zones are annual culture, and this region is unusual in having its own extension crop profile: Virginia Cooperative Extension's Specialty Crop Profile is the anchor for the whole band. Its system is the inverse of the northern one and worth understanding before you plant, because the chilling happens AFTER planting rather than before. Transplants go out at or a week or two before the last frost so the seedlings pick up 190 to 240 hours at or below 50°F in the ground, which is why the planting date is pinned to frost rather than chosen for convenience. Both zones are grown as an annual because the planting does not persist, and the measured overwintering is poor. The two zones differ in what limits them: zone 7 is a straightforward spring-planted annual, while zone 8 is warm enough that summer heat rather than winter is the binding constraint, which is why Virginia recommends its middle and upper Piedmont and mountains for this crop and advises against its own southern tier counties outright.

Bud tissue begins to freeze at about 29.9°F, which blisters and bronzes the outer bracts without affecting eating quality, and UC notes mature plants usually survive heavy frosts with reduced yield. our_prose: Arugula is a fast-growing, cool-season salad green with a peppery, mustardy flavor. It is one of the quickest things you can grow, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks, and it handles frost and even grows through winter in mild areas. Its main quirk is that it bolts (sends up a flower stalk) very fast in heat and long days, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter when it does. So it grows best in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, and in hot places it is a fall-to-spring crop. Sow a little every couple of weeks for a steady supply. It is easy and beginner-friendly; the main pest to watch is the flea beetle, which chews tiny holes in the leaves. There is also a wild kind of arugula that is slower to bolt and even more peppery.

our_prose: Arugula (Eruca sativa), also called salad rocket or roquette, is a fast, cool-season leafy green in the mustard family (Brassicaceae), grown for its tender, peppery leaves. It is one of the quickest crops in the garden, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks and full leaves in around a month, and it germinates readily even in cool soil and tolerates frost, so it can be sown very early and overwinters in mild zones. Its defining habit is how fast it bolts: heat above about 75°F and lengthening days send it to seed quickly, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter as it does, so the spring window is short, fall is the main crop, and in hot regions it is grown through the cool fall, winter, and spring. A separate wild or perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, sold as Sylvetta) is slower, more pungent, and far slower to bolt. Arugula is easy, succession-sown every 2 to 3 weeks, and a strong first-season choice, though flea beetles are its signature pest.

our_prose: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), arugula is a fast spring-and-fall succession green built around frost. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since arugula tolerates frost and even germinates in cool soil, and sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks for a steady supply. our_prose: Banana pepper is a warm-season vegetable in the same family as tomatoes and eggplant, grown for its long, tapered fruit that ripens from pale yellow to orange and red. The name covers two kinds that look almost the same: sweet banana peppers are mild, and hot Hungarian wax peppers are spicy and get hotter as they ripen, so it helps to know which you planted. Like most peppers you can pick them at two stages: yellow, or left on the plant to color up and sweeten (or, for the hot ones, get hotter). Banana peppers are heavy producers, they pollinate themselves so one plant will fruit, and they take cool weather a little better than big bell peppers, though they still love warmth and are grown from transplants set into warm soil. They are only light feeders, so going heavy on fertilizer gives you a big leafy plant with few peppers. The two things to watch are blossom-end rot, a dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit caused by uneven watering, and sunscald, a pale burned patch on peppers left exposed to strong sun. In very hot weather the flowers drop and the plant stops setting fruit for a while, so in hot climates peppers are grown in spring and fall with a summer break. The main things to get right are warmth, steady and even watering with mulch, modest fertilizer, full sun, and rotating peppers away from where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew.

our_prose: Banana peppers can be picked at TWO stages, and the choice is yours. The sweet banana types are most often harvested at their pale, waxy yellow stage, once the long, tapered fruit is full-size and firm; you do not need to wait for color. Left on the plant, the same fruit ripens on through orange to red, growing noticeably sweeter over the following weeks. Picking fruit at the yellow stage keeps the plant flowering and setting more, while letting fruit color up ties up the plant's energy and slows further set. Cut peppers with pruners or a knife leaving a short stub of stem, rather than pulling, because the branches are brittle and snap easily. Banana peppers are heavy setters, so pick often. Watch fruit left to color for anthracnose and sunscald if the weather turns hot, wet, or intensely sunny. If you are growing the hot Hungarian wax types, remember the heat climbs as the fruit ripens toward red.

our_prose: Sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum) is the most economically important annual culinary herb grown in North America, and its defining biology shapes every care decision. It is frost-tender without reservation: chilling injury begins below 50 °F, and a single frost kills the plant entirely. This means the growing window is bounded by last frost on one end and first frost on the other, making basil one of the most zone-sensitive herbs in the kitchen garden. Grown for leaves, not fruit, the central challenge is delaying the reproductive bolt: once basil shifts to flower production, leaf yield drops and essential oil concentration changes, altering flavor. The management lever is regular pinching of shoot tips and emerging flower buds, which redirects energy back into vegetative growth and can extend productive leaf harvest by weeks. Basil is a high-reward succession crop; successive plantings every 3 weeks from last frost through midsummer ensure a constant supply of young, tender growth. The herb is also one of the most container-friendly crops in this dataset, performing well in a single well-draining pot on a sunny windowsill or patio, which opens the season in all zones.

our_prose: California's desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella Valleys) are excellent for basil through spring and summer. UC ANR confirms basil thrives in the hot, dry desert summer climate. Plant out in mid-March through April once last frost has passed; zone 10 desert areas may plant as early as late February. The intense afternoon sun in peak summer (often exceeding 110°F) benefits from partial afternoon shade cloth or an east-facing orientation, but this is a management adjustment, not a planting pause. Basil continues growing productively through summer with consistent irrigation. Three to four succession plantings from March through June extend the harvest season and replace plants that eventually bolt. Harvest continues through November in zone 9 and into December or beyond in the warmest zone 10 desert areas. Downy mildew pressure is low in this dry climate; Fusarium wilt in warm, moist soil is the primary disease concern.

our_prose: Florida's peninsula supports basil in two main arms: a spring arm (February-May in zone 10; March-May in zone 11) and a fall arm (September-October). The summer rainy season (June-September) creates high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness that strongly favors basil downy mildew, making summer the most challenging time to maintain quality. Spring arm plants are best harvested through June before rainy season peaks; fall arm plants planted after the rains ease in September produce into December (zone 10) or beyond (zone 11). UF/IFAS calendars recommend planting heat-loving herbs including basil in both April-May and September-October windows. In zone 11 (South Florida), basil can grow almost continuously with proper disease management during the wet season. Overhead watering should be avoided entirely in Florida; drip or base watering is essential to limit the leaf wetness that drives downy mildew. Resistant varieties (Devotion, Obsession, Prospera) are particularly important in this high-humidity environment.

our_prose: Bee balm's companion role is the pollinator-magnet inversion: it is the plant you site to benefit others. our_prose: California's desert valleys (Imperial, Coachella) grow beefsteak on an inverted, two-window calendar driven by extreme summer heat. The main crop is set out across the cool season, December through March, to mature and set fruit before summer; a second fall crop goes out in early fall (about September) as the heat breaks and produces into the mild winter. June through August is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: complete blossom drop for every tomato type, not narrowed for beefsteak, which is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry. Confirm local frost for the winter harvest tail. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

our_prose: California's interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin) grow beefsteak as a single long warm season: set transplants out April into May and harvest from midsummer into fall up to first frost. UC ANR lists one April-May tomato window with no separate fall planting, so this is one continuous crop, not a spring-and-fall split. Large-fruited beefsteak sets fewer fruit through the peak-heat weeks of the valley summer (it is more heat-sensitive than cherry types), with set resuming as nights cool; the plant stays in the ground through the dip. Cages suit the valley heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

our_prose: California's North and North Coast (Monterey County north) grow beefsteak as a single cool-limited season: set transplants out in May once daytime temperatures are reliably above 70 °F, and harvest from late summer into fall. Large-fruited beefsteak needs warm days to ripen and can be slow in the coolest coastal pockets, so choose a variety matched to your season length and give it the warmest, most sheltered exposure. our_prose: Beets give you two harvests. You can pick the leaves young all along, taking a few outer ones per plant so the root keeps growing, and the seedlings you thin out are your first baby greens. The roots are ready by size, not a set date: brush the soil off a shoulder and pull when the beet is about 1 1/2 to 2 inches across, the sweet, tender stage, usually around 50 to 70 days. You can let them grow up to about 3 inches, but bigger beets get woody and strong. There is no rush in cool weather: they get sweeter after a light frost and hold in the ground, and the roots take more cold than the leaves. In cold areas, pile straw over the row and dig them into early winter until the ground freezes. Pull by hand, or loosen with a fork in heavy soil, and twist off the tops, leaving an inch of stem on beets you want to store so they do not bleed out their color.

our_prose: Direct-sow beets into the garden; they resent transplanting and are simplest grown from seed in place. Sow about 1/2 inch deep once the soil is workable and at least 45 to 50°F, roughly 2 to 3 weeks before the last spring frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop. Soaking the seed in warm water for about 24 hours before sowing speeds the slow germination. The key beet-specific point is that each beet seed is a multigerm seedball, a dried fruit containing several embryos, so a single seed sprouts a small cluster of seedlings and the stand must be thinned. Monogerm cultivars (one seedling per seed) avoid this. Keep the surface moist and uncrusted until the seedlings emerge, often 1 to 2 weeks.

our_prose: Bell pepper is a warm-season vegetable in the same family as tomatoes and eggplant, grown for its sweet, blocky fruit. The nice thing about peppers is you can pick them at two stages: green and full-size, or left on the plant to ripen to red, orange, yellow, or purple and turn sweeter. Peppers pollinate themselves, so one plant will fruit, and they love warmth, so you grow them from transplants set into warm soil once the nights are mild. They are only light feeders, so going heavy on fertilizer gives you a big leafy plant with few peppers. The two things to watch are blossom-end rot, a dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit caused by uneven watering, and sunscald, a pale burned patch on peppers left exposed to strong sun. In very hot weather the flowers drop and the plant stops setting fruit for a while, so in hot climates peppers are grown in spring and fall with a summer break. The main things to get right are warmth, steady and even watering with mulch, modest fertilizer, full sun, and rotating peppers away from where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew.

our_prose: Bell peppers can be picked at TWO stages, and the choice is yours. Most are harvested GREEN and full-size, once the fruit is firm, blocky, and has thick, glossy walls; you do not need to wait for color. Left on the plant, the same fruit ripens through to its final red, orange, yellow, or purple, growing noticeably sweeter and richer in vitamins over the next two to three weeks. Ripening on the plant ties up the plant's energy, so picking peppers green keeps it flowering and setting more, while letting fruit color up slows further production. Cut peppers with pruners or a knife leaving a short stub of stem, rather than pulling, because the branches are brittle and snap easily. Harvest green types regularly, and watch colored fruit for anthracnose and sunscald if you leave it to ripen in hot, wet, or intensely sunny weather.

our_prose: Cane management is the heart of growing blackberries, because the crown and roots are perennial but each cane is biennial: it grows one year as a primocane, fruits the next as a floricane, then dies. How you prune depends on both habit and cane type. On ERECT SUMMER-BEARING types, tip the primocanes at 3 to 4 feet in summer to force fruiting laterals; the next year those canes fruit as floricanes and then die, so cut spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest, and in late winter shorten the laterals to 12 to 18 inches and thin to 4 to 6 sturdy canes per foot of row. Erect types also sucker from the roots and need their spread contained to the row. On SEMI-ERECT and TRAILING types, which form a crown and do not sucker, train the long primocanes onto a trellis through the season, remove spent floricanes after harvest, and in late winter shorten laterals (about 10 to 12 inches on semi-erect) and keep 6 to 8 strong canes per crown. On PRIMOCANE-FRUITING (everbearing) types, the first-year canes fruit on their tips in late summer and fall; the simplest management is to mow every cane to the ground in late winter for one clean, heavy fall crop with the easiest pruning and reduced disease and borer pressure. The same planting can instead be double-cropped, leaving the lower canes to fruit again as floricanes the next summer, but the single-crop mow is the usual home choice.

our_prose: Blackberries are hardy in roughly zones 5 to 9, less cold-tolerant than raspberries but far more heat-tolerant, which is why they are the caneberry of the South. Cold hardiness follows habit: erect and semi-erect types are the toughest (Illini Hardy, Apache, and Chester are the standouts, reliable to about zone 5 and the edge of zone 4), while trailing types (marionberry, boysenberry) are the most tender and can be injured below about 13 °F, suiting them to mild coastal regions. In the far North (zones 3 to 4) blackberries are marginal and need winter protection; at the warm end, low-chill types thrive through the Deep South, and only the frost-free tropics push past their need for winter chill.

our_prose: Bok choy bolts two ways, and both close the eating window. A spell of cold on young plants, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, vernalizes them so they run to seed once it warms (UMN), and separately heat with long days drives a mature plant to flower. our_prose: Your spring planting bolted while still immature, sending up a seedstalk instead of building a rosette. This is vernalization (cold-induced) bolting: a young bok choy plant exposed to a prolonged cold spell, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, is cued to flower once warmth returns (UMN). our_prose: Broccoli microgreens are the young seedlings of broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica), harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage about 8 to 12 days after sowing. They are grown indoors year-round in a short repeatable cycle: a dense, dry, even sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat (broccoli needs no presoak), a brief dark blackout of about 3 to 4 days to drive even germination and stem stretch, then light to green up, then a single cut. The flavor is mild, fresh, and faintly cabbage-like. Broccoli is one of the most popular microgreens for nutrition; like other brassica microgreens it concentrates the glucosinolates that give the cabbage family its character, and research finds microgreens generally higher in vitamins and phytochemicals than the mature vegetable. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere.

our_prose: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. On the southern California coast the mild winter is the growing season and midsummer is too warm for firm sprouts, so brussels sprouts are planted in fall for a winter-into-spring harvest and the hottest months are excluded. (UC Master Gardeners San Diego County; UC IPM)

our_prose: In cold regions, brussels sprouts are a single long-season crop. Start seeds indoors in spring, plant them out in late spring or early summer, and let them grow all summer; the sprouts form as fall cools and taste best after frost. Harvest from the bottom of the stalk up through fall and into early winter. Deep winter cold eventually ends the crop.

our_prose: In the Southeast, brussels sprouts are a fall and winter crop, not a summer one. Start seeds indoors in mid-summer and set transplants out in late summer or early fall once the worst heat eases. Harvest through the mild winter into spring; frost makes the sprouts sweeter. Skip the hot summer, when the plants grow poorly and aphids are bad. Note that brussels sprouts are a minor, somewhat challenging crop in the Deep South because the cool window is short.

our_prose: Harvest butternut once at full maturity, not young: wait for a deep, solid tan or buff rind with no green streaks, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, and a dried, corky stem. The skin turns from glossy to dull at ripeness. Butternut colors tan well before it is mature, so give it the extra time: UMass notes the rind turns tan around 45 days after fruit set but the squash should hang on the vine about two more weeks. Cut the fruit from the vine with shears or a knife, leaving a 1 to 2 inch handle of stem, and avoid carrying it by the stem. Get the crop in before a hard frost, which damages the rind and shortens storage. Then cure the squash about 10 days in a warm, dry spot to harden the skin before storing.

our_prose: Calendula, also called pot marigold, is an easy, cheerful flower for cool weather. It is not the same plant as the marigolds you may know (those are a different plant called Tagetes). Calendula handles light frost, blooms in the cool parts of the year, spring and fall, and right through winter in mild-winter areas, but it fades and stops flowering in hot summer weather. The gold and orange petals are edible and add color to food, and the flowers have long been used in skin creams and salves. our_prose: Dark brown to black, irregularly shaped spots with yellow halos appear first on the older, lower leaflet margins and tips; this is Alternaria dauci. Tan to gray circular spots with darker margins, showing on younger leaves and earlier in the season, point to the closely related Cercospora carotae. As the spots multiply they run together and the foliage takes on a scorched, blighted look, and large lesions can girdle and kill the petioles. The two fungi are difficult to tell apart and are managed identically. The roots are not infected directly but size up poorly when the canopy is badly damaged. A third, bacterial blight (Xanthomonas campestris pv. carotae), looks similar, with water-soaked, varnished lesions that track down the veins.

our_prose: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder, and steady fertility matters even more than with other cole crops because a hungry plant buttons, forming a tiny premature curd instead of a full one. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, using roughly 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate. our_prose: Cauliflower is almost always transplanted, since precise timing and an unstressed start matter so much. For spring, start seeds indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before set-out and transplant sturdy young plants out around 2 weeks before the last frost; cauliflower transplants are less cold-hardy than cabbage or broccoli, so do not rush them into hard cold. For fall, start indoors or direct sow in early-to-mid summer and set out so the curd matures in cool fall weather. The single biggest transplant mistake is setting out an old, root-bound, or cold-checked plant: that stress triggers buttoning, where the plant forms a tiny premature curd. Set out stocky plants with 4 to 6 true leaves, harden them off over 7 to 10 days, and keep them growing without a stall.

our_prose: Plant a second compatible variety unless you choose a self-fertile one. Most sweet cherries are self-incompatible: a lone Bing sets no crop. our_prose: The desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) grow cherry tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar built around a hard summer heat exclusion. The main crop is transplanted in the mild winter window, December through mid-March, and harvested from spring into June; then June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs past 95°F and often above 110°F, which collapses viable pollen), so planting pauses. A second, fall crop is set out in September as the heat breaks and produces through the mild desert winter into January. This summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by cherry's heat resistance: unlike the milder southeastern Gulf summer, desert peak heat stops fruit set even for heat-tolerant cherry types. Confirm local frost and heat timing, which vary across the desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

our_prose: The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run well past 95°F and often above 110°F, and tomato flowers fail to set fruit once temperatures stay above about 95°F (high heat reduces viable pollen). Unlike the milder southeastern summer, this desert pause is climatic-absolute: it is wide and is not narrowed by cherry's heat resistance, because even heat-tolerant cherry types cannot set fruit in extreme desert summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

our_prose: In California's interior valleys you plant cherry tomatoes once, in spring (April or May), and then pick them all the way through summer and into fall until the first frost. You do not plant a second fall crop the way gardeners do in hotter, more humid places, because here cherry tomatoes handle the summer heat well and just keep producing from that one planting. Wait to plant until the soil has warmed up, usually late April, even though the last frost is earlier.

our_prose: The interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar) grow cherry tomatoes as a single long season rather than the spring-and-fall split used in the humid Southeast. Transplants go out in April and May, after the mediterranean-climate last frost and once soil warms past about 65°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through the hot summer into fall up to first frost. our_prose: The North Coast (Monterey County north, including the cool marine-influenced counties such as Marin) grows cherry tomatoes as a single short warm season set by heat availability rather than frost. Transplants go out in May, later than the interior valleys, because coastal summers are cool and nights can sit below 55°F in any month. A single planting then carries one harvest through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten, ahead of the late coastal first frost. This is the cool-limited case: the limiting factor is insufficient summer heat, not a midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cool-summer-adapted varieties and the warmest, most sheltered sites do best, and microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

our_prose: The South Coast (San Luis Obispo County south, including the San Diego and Los Angeles basin coast) grows cherry tomatoes as a single long warm season. Transplants go out across a wide April through mid-July window, the longest planting window of the California regions, into a mild marine climate with no midsummer heat exclusion. A single planting then carries one continuous harvest: on the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year, while slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by fall cooling and the late or absent coastal frost rather than by summer heat, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cherry types are heat resistant and set well through the warm season; coastal microclimate varies, so confirm local conditions. our_prose: The Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11, south of about Orlando) grows cherry tomatoes on a single long cool-season window rather than the spring-and-fall pattern of cooler regions. Because frost is rare, the planting window runs continuously from the fall transplant in September and October through February, the last month UF/IFAS lists for planting tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Production carries through the mild winter and spring. The limiting season is summer: in July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) cause blossom drop and fruit-set failure. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; cherry types are heat resistant, so the exclusion narrows to those two peak months for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Start seed indoors in August for fall transplanting, and choose fast-maturing cherry types. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

our_prose: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows cherry tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Transplants go out a week or two after the last spring frost, once nights stay above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through summer until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: unlike the Southeast or the desert valleys, northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the winter gaps are frost pauses and the season is uninterrupted between them. Cherry types (55 to 65 days from transplant) are well suited to short seasons and ripen before first frost even in zone 3. The cold end (zones 3 and 4) leans on fast-maturing varieties and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters), while the warm end (zones 6 and 7) has room for a second transplanting in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

our_prose: Rotate nightshades to a fresh bed every 3 years minimum. Soilborne pathogens, particularly Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici), Verticillium wilt, and early blight (Alternaria solani), can persist in soil or on plant debris for multiple seasons. Fusarium and Verticillium are soil-systemic and resistant to most home-garden interventions once established; the primary management tool for the home gardener is rotation combined with resistant varieties. Avoid planting tomatoes after any Solanaceae crop (peppers, eggplant, potatoes), as these share the same pathogen suite.

our_prose: Stop high-nitrogen feeding when flowers appear and switch to a high-potassium, low-nitrogen feed. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth by stimulating cell division and chlorophyll synthesis, exactly what you want early in the season and exactly what you don't want once flowering starts; potassium plays a different role: it regulates stomatal opening, drives sugar transport from leaves into developing fruit, and is critical for cell wall formation in the fruit itself. A tomato-specific or high-K fertilizer (look for an NPK ratio with a high last number, such as 5-10-10 or 4-12-8) used from first flowering onward translates directly into heavier, better-flavored fruit.

our_prose: Chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are a hardy, clump-forming perennial in the onion family (Amaryllidaceae), grown for their slender, hollow, grass-like leaves and their edible pink to pale purple pom-pom flowers. Unlike the annual and biennial kitchen herbs, chives are planted once and come back on their own year after year: the clump dies back to the ground over winter, rests dormant, and pushes up fresh green blades as one of the very first herbs of spring. They are among the hardiest herbs grown, reliable to roughly USDA zone 3, and among the easiest, with a mild onion flavor and few real pests. Give them full sun to light shade, average to rich well-drained soil, and steady moisture, though an established clump tolerates short dry spells. The clumps slowly widen from year to year and are best lifted and divided every 2 to 3 years to keep them vigorous. Chives are cool-preferring: in cold regions they run right through the northern summer, while in the hot South and desert they are a cool-season herb that slows or rests in the worst summer heat and revives as it cools. A close relative, garlic chives (Allium tuberosum), is a distinct species with flat leaves, a mild garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers.

our_prose: Chives come in two distinct plants. Common chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are the familiar fine, hollow-leaved clump with pink-purple spring flowers and a mild onion taste; named selections differ mostly in leaf fineness and vigor, from the slender Fine Leaf and Grolau strains favored for pots and forcing, to the thick, easy-cutting Staro, to taller showy-flowered Forescate. Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) are a separate species with flat leaves, a garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers; they are tougher in heat and drought but self-sow aggressively. All are grown much the same way, so choice comes down to flavor (onion versus garlic), leaf form, and how much you value the flowers, while any chive self-seeds if you let the blooms set seed.

our_prose: Cilantro is not one of USU Extension's Table 1 vegetable rows, so this spring window follows the Group A (Hardy) February 15 date given to St. George's other cold-hardy, quick-germinating spring crops. Leaves are ready in about 60 days; cilantro's own heat threshold runs around 75°F, one of the lowest of this family's herbs, so the plant bolts to coriander seed early once the season warms. our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs cucumbers on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 58 days later, around May 12, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, vines stop setting fruit and any that does form turns bitter. USU documents fall planting for cool-season crops in the St. George area but gives no fall or summer-replant window for cucumbers, so there is no second cycle here; frost returns around November 1, well after the plants have already stopped producing for the year.

our_prose: Edamame is a soybean you eat as plump green pods, boiled or steamed in the pod and popped straight into your mouth. It grows like a bush bean: you plant the seeds in the garden after the last frost once the soil is warm, and the sturdy plants need no trellis. But edamame takes longer than green beans, about 75 to 100 days, and the big difference is that the whole plant ripens at once. Instead of picking for weeks, you harvest the whole plant in one go when the pods are plump and green, and the best window is only a few days. Soybeans flower by day length, so pick a variety suited to your area, and use a soybean inoculant on the seed, not the regular bean kind. Always cook edamame before eating it.

our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs English cucumbers on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 60 days later, around May 14, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, vines stop setting fruit and any that does form turns bitter. our_prose: Field corn, also called dent corn, is a tall grass grown not for fresh eating but for the hard, dry grain inside the ear. You let the ears ripen and dry right on the stalk, then shell off the kernels to grind into cornmeal, grits, or masa for tortillas, or to feed to livestock and poultry. Old open-pollinated types like John Haulk and Cocke's Prolific can tower up to 15 feet, while modern grain hybrids are shorter and faster. Like all corn it is pollinated by wind, so you plant it in a square block of short rows, not a single line, so the tassels can dust the silks and fill the ears. One important warning: field corn pollen will drift into nearby sweet corn or popcorn and ruin them, turning sweet kernels starchy and keeping popcorn from popping, so keep them at least 300 feet apart or time your plantings so they tassel about two weeks apart.

our_prose: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a hardy allium grown from individual cloves planted in fall. It roots before winter, overwinters in the ground (mulched in cold regions), then resumes growth in spring and matures the following summer, an eight to nine month crop that spans the year. Winter cold is essential: cloves must be vernalized to divide and bulb properly, which is why fall planting beats spring. Hardneck types suit cold winters, produce edible scapes, and store a few months; softneck types suit mild climates, braid well, and store the longest.

our_prose: Garlic has a moderate to high nitrogen demand and builds its bulb on the leaves it grows in spring, so feeding is front-loaded onto the spring vegetative push. Mix a complete fertilizer or compost into the bed at fall planting, then side-dress nitrogen as the shoots resume growth in early spring and again two to three weeks later. The exact cutoff tracks your season rather than a fixed calendar date. In cold-winter regions with a later crop, the last feedings run later: Utah State suggests about half a pound of 21-0-0 per 100 square feet in mid-April with a quarter pound in late May, and the University of Minnesota feeds through spring growth before bulbing. In the warm Southeast, where the crop runs weeks earlier, UGA advises no nitrogen after the first week of April. The unifying rule is to stop nitrogen several weeks before bulbing begins, since late feeding delays bulbing, thickens necks, and worsens storage.

our_prose: The desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) grow grape tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar built around a hard summer heat exclusion. The main crop is transplanted in the mild winter window, December through mid-March, and harvested from spring into June; then June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs past 95°F and often above 110°F, which collapses viable pollen), so planting pauses. A second, fall crop is set out in September as the heat breaks and produces through the mild desert winter into January. This summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance: unlike the milder southeastern Gulf summer, desert peak heat stops fruit set even for heat-tolerant grape types. Confirm local frost and heat timing, which vary across the desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

our_prose: The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run well past 95°F and often above 110°F, and tomato flowers fail to set fruit once temperatures stay above about 95°F (high heat reduces viable pollen). Unlike the milder southeastern summer, this desert pause is climatic-absolute: it is wide and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance, because even heat-tolerant grape types cannot set fruit in extreme desert summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

our_prose: In California's interior valleys you plant grape tomatoes once, in spring (April or May), and then pick them all the way through summer and into fall until the first frost. You do not plant a second fall crop the way gardeners do in hotter, more humid places, because here grape tomatoes handle the summer heat well and just keep producing from that one planting. Wait to plant until the soil has warmed up, usually late April, even though the last frost is earlier.

our_prose: The interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar) grow grape tomatoes as a single long season rather than the spring-and-fall split used in the humid Southeast. Transplants go out in April and May, after the mediterranean-climate last frost and once soil warms past about 65°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through the hot summer into fall up to first frost. Grape types are heat resistant and keep setting fruit through the peak valley heat better than large-fruited tomatoes, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop here. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC ANR)

our_prose: The North Coast (Monterey County north, including the cool marine-influenced counties such as Marin) grows grape tomatoes as a single short warm season set by heat availability rather than frost. Transplants go out in May, later than the interior valleys, because coastal summers are cool and nights can sit below 55°F in any month. A single planting then carries one harvest through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten, ahead of the late coastal first frost. This is the cool-limited case: the limiting factor is insufficient summer heat, not a midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cool-summer-adapted varieties and the warmest, most sheltered sites do best, and microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

our_prose: The South Coast (San Luis Obispo County south, including the San Diego and Los Angeles basin coast) grows grape tomatoes as a single long warm season. Transplants go out across a wide April through mid-July window, the longest planting window of the California regions, into a mild marine climate with no midsummer heat exclusion. A single planting then carries one continuous harvest: on the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year, while slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by fall cooling and the late or absent coastal frost rather than by summer heat, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Grape types are heat resistant and set well through the warm season; coastal microclimate varies, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

our_prose: The Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11, south of about Orlando) grows grape tomatoes on a single long cool-season window rather than the spring-and-fall pattern of cooler regions. Because frost is rare, the planting window runs continuously from the fall transplant in September and October through February, the last month UF/IFAS lists for planting tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Production carries through the mild winter and spring. The limiting season is summer: in July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) cause blossom drop and fruit-set failure. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; grape types are heat resistant, so the exclusion narrows to those two peak months for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Start seed indoors in August for fall transplanting, and choose fast-maturing grape types. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

our_prose: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows grape tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Transplants go out a week or two after the last spring frost, once nights stay above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through summer until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: unlike the Southeast or the desert valleys, northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the winter gaps are frost pauses and the season is uninterrupted between them. Grape types (65 to 75 days from transplant) are well suited to short seasons and ripen before first frost even in zone 3. The cold end (zones 3 and 4) leans on fast-maturing varieties and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters), while the warm end (zones 6 and 7) has room for a second transplanting in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs bush beans on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 55 days later, around May 9, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, blossoms drop and pods fail to set. USU documents fall planting for cool-season crops in the St. George area but gives no fall or summer-replant window for bush beans, so there is no second cycle here; frost returns around November 1, well after the plants have already stopped producing for the year.

our_prose: Open-pollinated, mostly indeterminate tomatoes grown for flavor and diversity. The defining trait of an heirloom is that it is open-pollinated: it breeds true from saved seed, so a Brandywine grown from last year's seed comes back as Brandywine, unlike an F1 hybrid whose saved seed segregates into a mix of the parent traits. Heirlooms span an enormous range of size, color, and shape, from the dusky Cherokee Purple and Black Krim, to the green-when-ripe Green Zebra, to two-pound pink Brandywine and Hillbilly slicers, to open-pollinated paste types like San Marzano and Amish Paste. Most classic heirlooms are indeterminate: the vine keeps extending and setting fruit until frost, so it needs strong staking or caging and benefits from pruning to one or two main stems. Days to maturity vary widely by variety, roughly 70 to 90 days from transplant. The main tradeoff is disease: heirlooms generally lack the Verticillium, Fusarium, and nematode resistance (the VFN codes) bred into modern hybrids, so they are more prone to the soilborne wilts, to early and late blight and Septoria leaf spot, and to fruit cracking, and they reward attentive rotation, sanitation, and even watering. Like all tomatoes they need a long frost-free window and set fruit poorly once day temperatures pass the upper 80s°F or nights stay above about 70°F.

If you've never tested your soil, an inexpensive test kit from a garden center is worth doing before your first season. Many extension offices also offer low-cost testing.

our_prose: California's desert valleys (Imperial, Coachella) grow heirloom on an inverted, two-window calendar driven by extreme summer heat. The main crop is set out across the cool season, December through March, to mature and set fruit before summer; a second fall crop goes out in early fall (about September) as the heat breaks and produces into the mild winter. June through August is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: complete blossom drop for every tomato type, not narrowed for heirloom, which is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry. Confirm local frost for the winter harvest tail. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

our_prose: California's interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin) grow heirloom as a single long warm season: set transplants out April into May and harvest from midsummer into fall up to first frost. UC ANR lists one April-May tomato window with no separate fall planting, so this is one continuous crop, not a spring-and-fall split. Large-fruited heirloom sets fewer fruit through the peak-heat weeks of the valley summer (it is more heat-sensitive than cherry types), with set resuming as nights cool; the plant stays in the ground through the dip. Cages suit the valley heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

our_prose: California's North and North Coast (Monterey County north) grow heirloom as a single cool-limited season: set transplants out in May once daytime temperatures are reliably above 70 °F, and harvest from late summer into fall. our_prose: Honeydew is a heat-loving, long-season trailing melon (Cucumis melo, Inodorus Group) grown for its smooth-skinned, sweet, pale flesh, a warm-season cousin of cantaloupe, cucumber, and squash. Of the common melons it wants the most heat and the longest season, roughly 85 to 100 warm days, and it is more cold-sensitive than cantaloupe, so cool-summer northern and coastal areas are marginal to unsuitable. It is harvested once at full ripeness and does not sweeten further off the vine, so reading the plant is the whole game, and it is harder to read than cantaloupe. our_prose: Jalapeno is a warm-season fruiting vegetable (Capsicum annuum), the most popular hot pepper in American gardens, grown for its firm, medium-hot pods. Its culture is that of any pepper, close to a bell: a heat-loving, self-fertile, transplant crop set into warm soil after frost, growing slowly until the ground is truly warm, then bearing continuously through the summer. What sets it apart is pungency. Jalapeno carries capsaicin, roughly 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville units, produced in glands on the placenta inside the pod, and its heat is not fixed: it rises as the fruit ripens from green to red and as the plant meets stress, especially heat and a controlled water pull, so the same variety can be mild or fiery depending on how and when it is grown and picked. Two jalapeno-specific points reassure new growers: corking, the fine tan netting on a mature pod's skin, is a prized sign of quality, not a defect; and pods can be picked firm and dark green (the usual harvest, around 70 to 80 days from transplant) or left to ripen red for more heat and sweetness. Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and pauses fruit set when days climb above about 90°F and nights above 75°F, so in the hottest regions the crop splits into a spring and a fall flush around the peak of summer. Its pests are aphids (and the mosaic viruses they carry), flea beetles on seedlings, the pepper maggot (which largely spares thin-walled hot types), the pepper weevil in the South, and hornworms; its main diseases are bacterial spot, mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, and anthracnose, all held off by clean seed, rotation, warm well-drained soil, and dry foliage. Handle the harvest with gloves: capsaicin is an oil that burns skin and eyes.

our_prose: Central and south Florida are hard country for lavender, and the honest guidance is to keep expectations low. UF/IFAS is clear that lavender is a Mediterranean plant that grows best in Florida's cooler seasons and that the state's high humidity brings fungal root rot. Across the peninsula it is a container or raised-bed plant, not a landscape perennial: plant in sharply drained mix, give afternoon shade against the intense sun, mulch the crown in winter against cold wet soil, keep air moving, and choose only heat- and humidity-tolerant types such as Spanish lavender or the hybrid Phenomenal. Common English lavender reliably fails. In central Florida (zone 10) a well-tended container plant may persist for a few years before declining; in the deep south (zone 11) lavender is genuinely marginal and best treated as a short-lived, cool-season container novelty. Where it flowers, the flush comes in the cooler half of the year, roughly spring into summer.

Plant or divide at any time in full sun and rich, well-drained soil, and water steadily. our_prose: Lemongrass is tender and heat-hungry, and the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, marine-tempered summer is a genuinely marginal climate for it: the region's long frost-free window gives this crop plenty of time but not the sustained warmth it wants. Start a division, nursery plant, or rooted grocery-store stalk indoors about 8 weeks before last frost, then set it out about a week after frost once the soil has warmed; it will sulk in cold ground. Site it in the single warmest microsite available (a south wall or over paving), feed it hard through summer, and expect a smaller clump with thinner stalks than a hot-summer garden produces, more so on the cooler immediate coast (z9) than the valley interior (z8). Harvest stalks once they reach about half an inch thick. Because frost kills the top growth, do a heavy final harvest just before the first fall frost, then dig and pot a division to overwinter indoors in a bright window; this crop will not survive the region's winter outdoors.

our_prose: Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral and lower numbers are more acidic. Lettuce does best between 6.0 and 6.8, slightly acidic, because that is where the nutrients it needs are easiest for the roots to take up. our_prose: North-coast calendar is cool-limited and summer-inclusive (Table 13.2: February through August), the inverse of the heat-inverted interior and desert. our_prose: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for leaf lettuce: sow and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation and notes that leafy and semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations, especially under overhead sprinklers, while heading types are the seasonal, higher-elevation exception. The locally bred 'UH Manoa' (a Green Mignonette selection) and 'Anuenue' are the low-elevation standards; CTAHR describes Manoa as heat-tolerant, slow to bolt, and tip-burn resistant, grown year-round. The hot, long-day months bring a quality dip rather than a production gap: expect faster bolting and more tip-burn, managed with cultivar choice, roughly 40 percent afternoon shade at hot low-elevation sites (per CTAHR shade trials), and a move to higher elevation for head types. Germination falls off above about 81°F, so warm-season sowings benefit from primed seed or a cooler germination spot. Keep soil moisture steady; protect soft-leaved types from heavy rain. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164 (Lettuce Production Guidelines for Hawaii), HGV-2 (Lettuce for the Home Garden), and B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii).

our_prose: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), lettuce is a spring-and-fall crop built around frost, not heat. Start sowing in spring as soon as the soil warms to about 40°F, usually a few weeks before your last frost, and sow a short row every couple of weeks for a steady supply. Plant again in mid to late summer for a fall crop. Skip the hottest part of summer, when lettuce bolts (sends up a flower stalk) and turns bitter. For the most reliable results your first season, aim for the spring window from when the soil is workable into early summer, and a fall sowing in July or August depending on your zone, leaving roughly a month before your first frost so young leaves size up while it is still mild. Lettuce takes light frost in stride, so a fall crop can keep going right up to the first hard freeze.

our_prose: Region calendar is frost-governed and spring-centric, the standard (non-inverted) lettuce pattern the warm regions invert against. Two succession arms bracket the summer: a spring arm sown from the soil-40°F crossing (a few weeks ahead of last frost) through the bolt-driven close as sustained heat above about 75°F sets in, and a fall arm whose start is heat-floored to roughly July 1 in the coldest zones rather than a flat first-frost-minus-90, since the unclamped offset would fall in peak summer heat and cause germination failure (soil thermoinhibition above about 80°F). The fall arm targets fast-maturing looseleaf at the 30-day baby-leaf end, harvested through light frost rather than to a full head, so the latest viable sow sits about 30 days ahead of first frost with no extra hard margin. Per-arm sowing counts are derived per zone (not a fixed season cap) and range roughly 7 to 10 across zones 3 through 7. Frost is the governing constraint at both ends; summer heat is the interior limit. Spring-sow timing is anchored to MSU (cool-season germination minimum 35 to 40°F) and UMN (direct sow as soil reaches 40°F, 2 to 4 weeks before last frost); the fall arm and heat floor to UMN midsummer-planting guidance and USU (fall lettuce 50 to 75 days before maturity, light frost tolerated to 32°F), with NDSU corroboration for the coldest-zone fall window. In the milder cold zones (6 and 7), a cold frame or row cover extends the harvest several weeks past the outdoor season, with slow winter growth that holds the standing crop rather than expanding it; this is season extension under protection, not part of the default outdoor calendar (VCE and UMN give cold frames and row cover a two-to-four-week spring and fall extension).

our_prose: The mandarin (Citrus reticulata and its hybrids, including satsuma, clementine, and tangerine) is a subtropical evergreen fruit tree grown for small, sweet, loose-skinned, easy-to-peel fruit that is usually seedless. Its defining advantage over other sweet citrus is cold hardiness: satsuma is the most cold-tolerant of the commonly grown citrus, with mature trees withstanding brief lows near 15 to 20°F, notably colder than a navel orange, which lets in-ground mandarins reach zone 8 across the Gulf South and interior valleys. Early ripening (satsuma from fall) also gets the crop off the tree before the hardest winter cold. Mandarins need less summer heat than a navel to sweeten but want cool fall nights to color and drop acid, so they are marginal only in the cool-night tropics and the coolest coasts. Two group traits shape their care: seedless types set seeds if cross-pollinated by other citrus, so isolation preserves seedlessness; and mandarins are strongly alternate-bearing, managed by thinning heavy crops. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree and are picked promptly. Trees are small and grafted, usually on trifoliate-orange rootstock for cold hardiness, and productive for decades.

our_prose: Marigold inverts the usual companion framing: it is the plant you place to benefit others. Its one research-supported pest function is nematode suppression, and only in a specific form: French marigolds (Tagetes patula) grown as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months in the target bed and then incorporated, ahead of a susceptible crop, can reduce root-knot and lesion nematode populations via root-released alpha-terthienyl. UF/IFAS is explicit that simply interplanting a few marigolds among vegetables has not been shown to reduce nematodes, and the African types are less effective than French for this. The broader reputation, that marigold scent repels insects, rabbits, and deer, is traditional companion lore: sometimes borne out, not reliably documented. What is solid is that marigold is a strong pollinator and beneficial-insect draw, so it earns its place as an insectary edge or border. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site for sun and airflow.

our_prose: Choose by type and purpose. our_prose: Mulberry as a group spans a very wide climate range because three species and their hybrids cover it: white mulberry (Morus alba) and the hardy hybrids (Illinois Everbearing, Silk Hope) are cold-hardy to about zones 4 to 5 and up; red mulberry (Morus rubra), the native, runs roughly zones 4 to 9; and black mulberry (Morus nigra) and low-chill types are tender, warm-climate trees for about zones 7 to 10 and into the subtropics. our_prose: Okra companion pairings are largely traditional rather than trial-tested, and the useful ones fall into a few practical roles. As a tall, late, heat-loving Malvaceae, okra does not share the disease load of tomatoes and other nightshades, so it makes a good rotational and bed neighbor for them rather than a competitor for the same soil pests. Southern peas and other legumes are a long-standing Southern partner, fixing nitrogen and, in the case of cowpeas, acting as a trap that pulls stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs off the pods. Quick crops like lettuce and radish use the open ground while young okra is small, and flowering insectary plants draw the bees and beneficial insects that help. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep okra away from cotton, hibiscus, and other mallows, which share its root-knot nematode and fusarium problems.

our_prose: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 to 7), onion is a single spring-planted crop. Grow long-day cultivars: they need 14 to 16 hours of daylight to bulb, which northern summers deliver, and they build a full leaf canopy before the solstice trigger so bulbs size up large. Start seed indoors about 10 weeks ahead (sow in February for a May transplant in the coldest zones), then set cold-hardy transplants or sets out as soon as the soil is workable, roughly two weeks before the last frost. Bulbs mature in mid-to-late summer when about half the tops fall over; lift and cure them two to four weeks before storage. Day length gates which cultivar bulbs here, not when you plant: planting stays anchored to frost and workable soil. The bolting trap here is cold-driven, not day-length driven, so it stays minor for a spring crop set as a small transplant, but oversized sets exposed to a cold snap can run to seed instead of bulbing.

our_prose: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 to 9), onion is a fall-planted, overwintering short-day crop. Grow short-day cultivars: they bulb at only 10 to 12 hours of daylight, which the region's mild fall and winter provide. Start seed in early-to-mid fall, then set transplants or sets from November through February so the plant builds a strong leaf canopy over winter before short days trigger bulbing. Bulbs mature in mid-spring, harvested April into May before summer heat; lift when about half the tops fall and cure before storage. Day length gates which cultivar bulbs here, not when you plant. The central pitfall is bolting: a transplant or set that is too large going into winter cold vernalizes and runs to seed instead of bulbing, so use pencil-sized or smaller transplants and sets under half an inch.

our_prose: Oregano reaches the grower as several practical types. Greek oregano (Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum) is the hot, pungent kitchen standard and the type sold dried; Italian oregano (O. x majoricum, an oregano-marjoram hybrid) is milder and sweeter. Common or wild oregano (O. vulgare) is the hardiest and most vigorous but has variable, sometimes bland flavor, so taste before you rely on it. Hot & Spicy is an extra-pungent selection, Golden oregano (O. vulgare 'Aureum') is a bright-foliaged ornamental-culinary form, and Syrian oregano (O. syriacum) is the tender za'atar herb. One important caution: Mexican oregano (Lippia graveolens) is not a true oregano at all but a shrub in the verbena family, grown in hot climates for a similar, stronger flavor. our_prose: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is a hardy biennial herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae), grown for its flavorful, vitamin-rich leaves. Its biology is the mirror image of warm-season herbs like basil and the opposite of fast cool-season herbs like cilantro. Parsley is COOL-TOLERANT and FROST-HARDY, taking light freezes and overwintering in mild zones, yet it is also genuinely HEAT-TOLERANT: because it is a biennial that does not flower until its second year, it does NOT bolt from first-year summer heat the way cilantro does, so a single planting yields leaves spring through fall, and only the most extreme desert and subtropical summers slow it. That long, flexible season is the headline. The signature challenge is at the start: parsley seed germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, so growers soak it and wait. It is harvested cut-and-come-again from the OUTER stems, leaving the center to regrow for months. It comes in flat-leaf (Italian) types, with the stronger, sweeter flavor cooks prefer, and curly (French) types grown for garnish, plus Hamburg root parsley grown for an edible root. The one catch is the biennial cycle: an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, so parsley is sown fresh each year for the best leaves. Pests are few, chiefly the parsleyworm (the handsome black swallowtail caterpillar, often left for the butterflies) and aphids, and disease is minimal.

our_prose: Parsley is one of USU Extension's named Table 1 crops: St. George's Group B (Semi-Hardy) planting date is about March 1. The seed is notably slow, taking 2 to 5 weeks to germinate, and leaves are ready roughly 80 days after sowing, from late May. Parsley is more heat-tolerant than its cool-season herb neighbors and does not bolt in its first year, so the stand holds through June even as St. George's summer heat, which routinely reaches 100°F in July per USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation data, slows growth and toughens the leaves. A second direct sowing in early August, timed a little ahead of the quicker herbs to give this slower crop enough runway, follows USU's general fall-gardening guidance for restarting cool-season crops (Fall Gardening in the St. George Area); the fall stand is ready from mid-to-late October and, thanks to parsley's own frost tolerance down to about 10°F, carries a slow cut-and-come-again harvest on past the average November 1 first frost and right through winter, into late February ahead of the next spring sowing.

our_prose: Pawpaw (Asimina triloba) is a deciduous understory tree native to eastern North America and, in the Annonaceae (custard-apple) family, the largest edible fruit native to the continent. Its custardy, tropical-tasting fruit, a blend of banana, mango, and pineapple, ripens in late summer and fall and is so perishable it is almost never sold in stores. Growing it well means working with two unusual traits: it is self-incompatible and fly- and beetle-pollinated, so it needs two genetically distinct trees and often hand pollination to set fruit; and as a woodland understory native, its young foliage wants part shade the first year or two before it takes full sun. It is very cold-hardy across roughly zones 5 to 8, spreads by root suckers into clonal patches, and is notably free of the pests and diseases that plague other fruit trees, with deer avoiding its foliage.

our_prose: Choose pawpaw varieties differently from other fruit trees: the first rule is genetic diversity, not chill matching. our_prose: A long-lived deciduous fruit tree (Pyrus pyrifolia) grown for round, crisp, apple-shaped fruit, also called the apple pear, sand pear, or nashi. Asian pear is a cross-pollination crop: nearly all cultivars are self-unfruitful, so you plant two different, bloom-overlapping varieties and rely on bees to move pollen between them (a couple, like Shinseiki and 20th Century, are partially self-fruitful but still crop far better with a pollinizer). The signature difference from the European pear is at harvest: Asian pears RIPEN ON THE TREE and are eaten crisp and juicy like an apple. You pick them tree-ripe and sweet, not firm-and-green to finish indoors, and a fruit picked too early stays hard and bland. The trees set very heavily and must be thinned hard for decent fruit size. Fire blight is the major disease, worst in warm, humid regions, so cultivar and rootstock choice matter. Chill requirement is moderate and variety-set (roughly 250 to 600 hours), and rootstock choice sets mature size and how soon the tree bears.

So plan to plant two different kinds of European pear, not two of the same, within about 50 to 100 ft of each other, and make sure they bloom at the same time. A couple of varieties (Bartlett, Anjou) can set a small crop on their own in mild areas, but even they do much better with a partner. Watch out for one famous mismatch: Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other, so give each of them a different partner like Bosc or Comice. And a few varieties (like Magness) cannot pollinate anything and need two partners themselves, so ask the nursery before you rely on one as your second tree.

our_prose: Pickling cucumbers come in three pollination habits, and it changes how you grow them. Monoecious open-pollinated types (such as Boston Pickling and National Pickling) carry separate male and female flowers on the same plant, so a single plant sets fruit, but each female needs several bee visits to size a fruit; early male flowers often open and drop before the first females appear, which is normal, and poor set in cool or pollinator-scarce weather shows up as small fruit that yellow and shrivel. Gynoecious hybrids (such as Calypso and Fancipak) are nearly all female and set a heavy, concentrated crop, but they need a pollenizer plant in the mix, which seed companies usually include in the packet as a few dyed seeds, so sow the whole packet together. Parthenocarpic types set seedless fruit with no pollination at all, which suits row covers, greenhouses, and containers. Plant flowers nearby and avoid spraying open blooms to keep pollinators working, and hand-pollinate with a small brush if set stalls.

our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs pickling cucumbers on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 53 days later, around May 7, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, vines stop setting fruit and any that does form turns bitter. USU documents fall planting for cool-season crops in the St. George area but gives no fall or summer-replant window for pickling cucumbers, so there is no second cycle here; frost returns around November 1, well after the plants have already stopped producing for the year.

our_prose: Pollination is the headline decision for plum, and it splits by type. European plums (Prunus domestica) such as Stanley, Italian prune, and damson are largely self-fruitful, so a single tree bears, though most crop somewhat more heavily with a second European variety nearby. Japanese plums (Prunus salicina) such as Santa Rosa, Burbank, and Methley are usually self-unfruitful and need a second compatible Japanese cultivar blooming at the same time; Methley and Santa Rosa are partial exceptions and also serve as good pollenizers. Crucially, European and Japanese plums bloom weeks apart and will not pollinate each other, so a pollenizer must match type. Plums are insect-pollinated, mainly by bees, so bloom-time pollinator activity matters; place a pollenizer within about 100 feet.

our_prose: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, with no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first so they do not stay dried out. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (that bumpy joint near the base, where the fruiting variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil you removed, water it in well, and add a stake only if the spot is windy.

our_prose: Pomegranate is the cold-tender member of this group: it survives winters across roughly zones 7 to 11 but is damaged by hard freezes. Standard cultivars like 'Wonderful' tolerate winter lows to about 10 to 15°F; the cold-hardy Russian types (Salavatski and kin) push to around 7°F, and a plant cut back by a severe freeze often resprouts from the base. It is also frost-sensitive in the shoulder seasons, before it is fully dormant in late fall and after buds swell in early spring. Surviving is only half the story: RELIABLE, well-colored fruit needs a long hot summer (roughly temperatures above 85°F for 120-plus days), so the dependable-fruit band is the hot-summer heart of zones 8 to 10. Zone 7 is the cold edge for hardy cultivars on protected sites, and the frost-free tropics (zone 11) are limited by humidity and too little chill or dry heat, not by cold.

our_prose: Pomegranate fruits reliably in the Rio Grande Valley: Valley winters easily clear its roughly 100-hour chill need, and Texas A&M AgriLife Extension reports fruiting types surviving most winters across central, southern, and southeastern Texas. This is a real, fruiting dooryard crop here, not just a survivor: the Valley is hot and considerably drier than the humid upper Gulf coast, roughly 20 to 27 inches of annual rainfall against the Gulf coast's 50 to 60, so it crops here much as it does in the low desert, where pomegranate is classically prime. An occasional wet late-summer spell can still cause some fruit splitting, but that is a modest, manageable risk, not the season-defining humidity problem of the wetter Gulf coast; favor an open, breezy, well-drained site and even irrigation. Exact Valley bloom and harvest months are not separately published by TAMU; this window is conservatively adapted from a reliably-fruiting desert pattern.

our_prose: Plant a dormant bare-root or potted pomegranate in late winter or early spring, after the worst cold and once the ground can be dug. Soak bare roots in water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots and set the plant at the same depth it grew before. Unlike a peach, a pomegranate is on its own roots with no graft joint to worry about. Decide now whether you want a bush with several trunks or a single small tree, and cut the plant back a bit to start it. If your soil is heavy or wet, plant on a raised mound. Fill in with the soil you dug out, water it well, and add mulch.

our_prose: The first year is about growing a strong plant, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root or potted young plant in late winter or early spring after the worst cold has passed, water it in, and decide the shape early: a natural bush with several trunks (keep three to six strong ones) or a single small tree (rub off the shoots that pop up from the base). Pomegranates send up lots of these base shoots (suckers), so pulling the extras is the main job the first year. Keep the young plant watered steadily through its first summer so the roots get going, and pick off any fruit that forms so the plant can focus on growing. Go easy on fertilizer, and avoid a lot of nitrogen, which grows leaves instead of fruit.

our_prose: Popcorn is a type of corn grown for its small, hard kernels that burst into fluffy popped corn when heated. Each kernel has a hard, moisture-sealed shell around a dense, starchy center; when it gets hot, the tiny bit of water trapped inside flashes to steam and the kernel explodes, turning itself inside out. You grow it just like other corn, in a square block of short rows so the wind can pollinate it, and you let the ears dry down on the stalk. Popular home types include the reliable yellow Robust hybrids, the tender heirloom Japanese Hulless, and ornamentals like deep-red Strawberry popcorn and blue-black Dakota Black that look as good on the shelf as they taste in the bowl. The single most important rule: keep popcorn away from all other corn, because pollen from sweet corn or field corn drifting onto your popcorn ruins its ability to pop. Keep them at least 300 feet apart, or time your plantings so they tassel about two weeks apart. Getting the kernels to the right dryness, about 13 to 14 percent moisture, is what makes them pop well.

our_prose: Popcorn (Zea mays var. everta) is a flint-type corn whose kernels carry an exceptionally hard, moisture-tight hull over a dense, glassy endosperm. When heated, the small amount of water sealed inside each kernel flashes to steam and pressure builds against the hard hull until it ruptures, and the gelatinized starch turns the kernel inside out into a crisp flake. That mechanism makes moisture the whole game: the ideal kernel moisture for popping is 13 to 14 percent, and kernels that are too wet pop small and chewy while kernels dried too far fail to pop at all. Representative types run from dependable modern yellow hybrids (the Robust series) and the classic tender heirloom Japanese Hulless to ornamentals like ruby Strawberry and blue-black Dakota Black that pop as well as they display. It is wind-pollinated and block-planted like any corn, a heavy nitrogen feeder with the same critical moisture window at tasseling and silking. Its isolation rule is the strictest of all the corns: because popping depends on an intact hard endosperm, any foreign pollen, sweet or dent, crossing onto the ear degrades the pop, so isolate by about 300 feet or stagger tasseling by roughly two weeks.

our_prose: Potatoes grow best in acidic soil, roughly pH 5.0 to 6.0, lower than most garden vegetables. The acidity is deliberate disease management: common scab (Streptomyces scabies) is suppressed in acidic soil and worsens as pH rises above about 5.5, especially in dry soil. Where scab is a recurring problem, hold the pH between about 5.0 and 5.3 and keep the soil evenly moist for the 4 to 9 weeks after planting when tubers are forming. Potatoes tolerate a wider band (down to about 4.8 and up to 6.5), and they will grow at neutral pH, but scab pressure climbs with pH, so do not lime a potato bed. A soil test removes the guesswork before planting.
