our_prose: Radishes bolt, sending up a flower stalk, as temperatures rise and days lengthen in late spring and early summer. Bolting is driven by heat and long days together, not by a cold-then-warm vernalization sequence, so it is mainly a late-spring and summer problem. A bolting radish turns its energy to the flower stalk: the root stops sizing, turns woody and pithy, and the flavor goes sharp and hot. Because the crop is fast, the practical fix is timing, growing radishes in the cool windows on either side of summer, with heat-tolerant or slow-bolt varieties for the late-spring edge.

our_prose: The maggots (young larvae) of the cabbage maggot fly, a small gray fly. our_prose: Cane management is the heart of growing raspberries, because the crown is perennial but each cane is biennial: it grows one year, fruits the next, then dies. How you prune depends entirely on the type. On SUMMER-BEARING (floricane-fruiting) raspberries, first-year primocanes grow vegetatively, overwinter, and fruit the following early summer as floricanes, then die; immediately after harvest cut those spent floricanes to the ground and remove them, and in late winter thin the surviving primocanes to 4 to 6 sturdy canes per foot of row, narrow the row to about a foot, and tie the canes to a trellis. On EVERBEARING (primocane-fruiting, or fall-bearing) raspberries, the first-year canes fruit on their tips in late summer or fall; the simplest and recommended management is to mow every cane to the ground in late winter for a single, clean, heavy fall crop with no training of overwintered canes and reduced disease and cane-borer pressure. The same everbearing planting can instead be double-cropped, leaving the lower canes to fruit again as floricanes the next summer, but the single-crop mow is far easier and the usual home choice. Red and yellow raspberries also sucker aggressively from the roots and need their spread contained to the row every season.

our_prose: Roma tomatoes, also called paste or plum tomatoes, are the ones you grow to make sauce. They differ from cherry tomatoes in an important way: a roma is a determinate plant, which means it grows to a bushy, compact size and then ripens most of its tomatoes within a few weeks, instead of giving you a handful at a time all summer. That is actually the point: you get a big batch all at once, perfect for cooking down into sauce or canning in one go. The fruit is egg-shaped, thick-walled, and meaty, with few seeds and not much juice, so it cooks down fast. Because the plant stays short, it needs a sturdy cage rather than a tall stake, and it barely needs pruning. The main thing to watch for is blossom-end rot, a dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit. It looks like a disease, but it is caused by uneven watering, so water steadily and mulch around the base. If you are in a cold zone (3 to 5), pick an early variety so the crop finishes before frost; in a warm zone (9 to 11) you can plant a second batch in late summer for more sauce tomatoes in fall.

our_prose: Roma tomatoes, also called paste or plum tomatoes, are the workhorse of the sauce and canning garden. Unlike the cherry class, roma is determinate: the plant grows to a compact, bushy size, sets most of its fruit in a few heavy clusters, and ripens that crop over a concentrated two to four week window rather than trickling out fruit all season. That concentrated set is the whole point, giving you a batch large enough to cook down into sauce, paste, or canned tomatoes in one or two sessions. The fruit is egg to plum shaped, meaty and dense, with thick walls, few seeds, and little juice, which is exactly what you want for cooking because there is less water to boil off. A determinate plant stays short enough to hold up in a sturdy cage rather than a tall stake, and it needs little to no pruning: clear the suckers below the first flower cluster and otherwise leave the plant full. The disorder roma growers fight most is blossom-end rot, a dark sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit driven by uneven calcium delivery when soil moisture swings; steady watering and mulch are the fix, not calcium sprays. In warm zones (9 to 11) a second planting extends the canning season; in short-season zones (3 to 5) choose an early paste variety so the concentrated set finishes before first frost.

our_prose: The desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) grow roma tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar built around a hard summer heat exclusion. The main crop is transplanted in the mild winter window, December through mid-March, and harvested from spring into June; then June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs past 95°F and often above 110°F, which collapses viable pollen), so planting pauses. A second, fall crop is set out in September as the heat breaks and produces through the mild desert winter into January. This summer pause is climatic-absolute: desert peak heat stops fruit set for roma as for any large-fruited tomato. Confirm local frost and heat timing, which vary across the desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

our_prose: In California's interior valleys you plant roma tomatoes once, in spring (April or May), and then pick them all the way through summer and into fall until the first frost. You do not plant a second fall crop the way gardeners do in hotter, more humid places, because here roma tomatoes handle the summer heat well and just keep producing from that one planting. Wait to plant until the soil has warmed up, usually late April, even though the last frost is earlier.

our_prose: The interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar) grow roma tomatoes as a single long season rather than the spring-and-fall split used in the humid Southeast. Transplants go out in April and May, after the mediterranean-climate last frost and once soil warms past about 65°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through the hot summer into fall up to first frost. Roma is a standard paste type without special heat tolerance, so fruit set slows in peak valley heat; there is still no separate fall crop, just a midsummer lull in set. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC ANR)

our_prose: The North Coast (Monterey County north, including the cool marine-influenced counties such as Marin) grows roma tomatoes as a single short warm season set by heat availability rather than frost. Transplants go out in May, later than the interior valleys, because coastal summers are cool and nights can sit below 55°F in any month. A single planting then carries one harvest through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten, ahead of the late coastal first frost. This is the cool-limited case: the limiting factor is insufficient summer heat, not a midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cool-summer-adapted varieties and the warmest, most sheltered sites do best, and microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

our_prose: The South Coast (San Luis Obispo County south, including the San Diego and Los Angeles basin coast) grows roma tomatoes as a single long warm season. Transplants go out across a wide April through mid-July window, the longest planting window of the California regions, into a mild marine climate with no midsummer heat exclusion. A single planting then carries one continuous harvest: on the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year, while slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by fall cooling and the late or absent coastal frost rather than by summer heat, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Roma sets fruit through the mild coastal warm season; coastal microclimate varies, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

our_prose: The Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11, south of about Orlando) grows roma tomatoes on a single long cool-season window rather than the spring-and-fall pattern of cooler regions. Because frost is rare, the planting window runs continuously from the fall transplant in September and October through February, the last month UF/IFAS lists for planting tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Production carries through the mild winter and spring. The limiting season is summer: in July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) cause blossom drop and fruit-set failure. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; roma types are heat resistant, so the exclusion narrows to those two peak months for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Start seed indoors in August for fall transplanting, and choose fast-maturing roma types. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

our_prose: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows roma tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Transplants go out a week or two after the last spring frost, once nights stay above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through summer until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: unlike the Southeast or the desert valleys, northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the winter gaps are frost pauses and the season is uninterrupted between them. Roma types (55 to 65 days from transplant) are well suited to short seasons and ripen before first frost even in zone 3. The cold end (zones 3 and 4) leans on fast-maturing varieties and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters), while the warm end (zones 6 and 7) has room for a second transplanting in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

our_prose: Rotate nightshades to a fresh bed every 3 years minimum. Soilborne pathogens, particularly Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici), Verticillium wilt, and early blight (Alternaria solani), can persist in soil or on plant debris for multiple seasons. Fusarium and Verticillium are soil-systemic and resistant to most home-garden interventions once established; the primary management tool for the home gardener is rotation combined with resistant varieties. Avoid planting tomatoes after any Solanaceae crop (peppers, eggplant, potatoes), as these share the same pathogen suite.

our_prose: Sage (Salvia officinalis), also called common, garden, or culinary sage, is a woody Mediterranean perennial subshrub in the mint family, grown for its aromatic, pebbly-textured, gray-green leaves used fresh or dried in cooking. This is the culinary kitchen sage, not the ornamental bedding salvias (such as scarlet or mealycup sage) sold as annual flowers. It carries short spikes of blue-purple flowers in early summer that bees and butterflies love, but the leaves are the crop, and many cooks pinch the flower spikes to keep the foliage flavorful. Sage thrives on lean treatment: full sun, poor to average well-drained soil, and little water or feeding. It is one of the hardier culinary herbs, reliably perennial in much of the country, but it is short-lived and turns woody and sprawling with age, so plan to replace plants every few years and prune each spring to slow the decline. Overwatering and humid heat, not cold, are what usually kill it, through root and stem rot.

our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs slicing cucumbers on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 63 days later, around May 17, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, vines stop setting fruit and any that does form turns bitter. USU documents fall planting for cool-season crops in the St. George area but gives no fall or summer-replant window for slicing cucumbers, so there is no second cycle here; frost returns around November 1, well after the plants have already stopped producing for the year.

our_prose: Harvest spaghetti squash once at full maturity, not young: wait for a deep, even golden-yellow rind with no green or cream tint, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, and a dried, corky stem. our_prose: A spring onion, also called a scallion or green onion, is a young onion you eat whole: the long white base and the green tops. You harvest it before it makes a round bulb, so it grows fast and is easy. Some kinds (called bunching onions) never make a bulb at all, and you can also just sow regular onions close together and pull them young as scallions. Plant the seeds shallow, thin the seedlings to about an inch apart, keep the soil damp, and they are usually ready in about 50 to 70 days, when the green tops are 6 to 8 inches tall. our_prose: In the cold-winter North, scallions are an easy cool-season crop you can grow from spring right through fall. On established June-bearing beds, do not feed in spring; spring nitrogen drives leaf growth, not fruit, and a dense canopy traps moisture and promotes gray mold. Instead, fertilize once at renovation, just after harvest, to build the flower buds for next year. Established day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all season, take the same total split into monthly doses through summer with an optional August feeding. On sandy soil, divide every rate into more frequent, lighter applications.

our_prose: The interior valley grows strawberries as a spring-cropping annual rather than a perennial bed, since summer heat and soilborne disease pressure cut productive life to one or two seasons. Short-day varieties planted in August do most of their fruiting the following spring, with harvest running from mid-April through mid-June and heaviest picking in May and June. Plants set in August may put out a small flush of blossoms the first fall, but removing those fall blossoms channels energy into crown development and produces a heavier spring crop. Replace the bed with fresh nursery stock every two to three years as heat and disease pressure accumulate. White mulch over the bed in summer keeps the soil cooler and reduces fruit burn once temperatures climb above 90°F.

our_prose: Florida is the winter strawberry capital, and in peninsular Florida (zones 10 and 11) strawberries are grown as a winter annual, not a perennial bed. Florida's fall, winter, and spring supply the cool temperatures (about 50°F to 80°F) and short days needed for flowering and fruit, while summer heat and rain exhaust the planting. Set bare-root or plug transplants in fall, from late September to early November (mid to late October in central and west-central Florida), on raised beds covered with black plastic mulch for drainage and clean fruit. Expect flowering from November and fruit in two or three cycles from late fall into April or May, then pull and discard the plants; the highest-quality fruit comes from young plants, so replant fresh each fall. Zone 10 can see a rare freeze that nips open blossoms, so keep frost cloth handy during bloom; zone 11 is frost-free. Rotate away from beds that grew strawberries, tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant in the past two to three years to limit soilborne disease.

our_prose: In the north (zones 3 to 7), strawberries are a perennial: you plant them once and the same bed comes back and fruits for several years. Plant the small brown dormant crowns in early spring, as soon as you can dig the soil, even if frost is still possible. June-bearing kinds give one big batch of berries in late spring or early summer, about a month after they bloom, then grow runners that root into new plants and fill the row. After the berries finish, cut the leaves back and thin the plants to keep the bed healthy, and start a fresh bed every three or four years. In zone 3, cover plants with straw over winter for protection; berries are most reliable from zone 4 and warmer.

our_prose: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam rich in organic matter. Because the roots are shallow and rot in waterlogged soil, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high on heavy or slow-draining ground. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting and adjust pH to 5.6 to 6.5 a season ahead, since sulfur or lime take months to act. Avoid ground that recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, which leave Verticillium wilt in the soil.

our_prose: There are three kinds of strawberries, and picking the right one matters more than picking a fancy variety. June-bearing types give you one big harvest over about four weeks in late spring or early summer, perfect if you want a pile of berries at once for jam or the freezer. They spread by sending out runners that fill in a wide row, and they give their first real crop the year after you plant them. Day-neutral types fruit a little at a time from late spring all the way to fall, give berries the first year, and stay compact, so they are the best choice for pots and small raised beds. Everbearing types fall in between, with one crop in early summer and another in late summer. This guide is built around the June-bearing kind grown in a wide row, since that is how most home gardeners grow strawberries, and it points out along the way where day-neutrals are handled differently. In mild coastal areas with gentle winters, day-neutral plants can give berries through much of the year, and gardeners there often plant fresh ones each year instead of keeping a bed for years.

our_prose: Strawberries come in three types, and the choice shapes your whole season. June-bearing cultivars set flower buds in the short days of fall and deliver one concentrated crop over about four weeks in late spring or early summer; they throw the most runners, so they suit a matted row and give a large flush ideal for freezing and jam. Their first real crop comes the season after planting. Day-neutral cultivars flower regardless of day length whenever temperatures sit between about 40 and 90°F, so they fruit from late spring through fall, bear in their first season, and throw few runners, which makes them the pick for containers, raised beds, and a steady supply of fresh berries. Everbearing cultivars give two lighter crops, one in early summer and one in late summer, and are generally less productive than day-neutrals. This guide follows the June-bearing matted-row model because it is the backbone of US backyard strawberry growing; the day-neutral notes throughout tell you where the care diverges. In mild-winter coastal regions, day-neutral plantings can fruit across much of the year and are often grown as a fall-set annual rather than a long-lived bed, which is why the warm-region notes treat them differently from the cold-region matted row.

our_prose: Sugar snap peas are an edible-pod pea grown for plump, rounded pods eaten whole, pod and peas together, while the pod is still crisp, bright, and sweet. They are the plump-podded cousin of the flat snow pea: where a snow pea is picked young and flat before its seeds develop, a snap pea is left until the peas inside have swelled and nearly filled the pod, giving the crunchy, sugary pod that names the type. Like all peas they are a cool-season legume, sown as early as the ground can be worked in spring and again for a fall crop, and they fix much of their own nitrogen. Types range from tall climbing vines that need a trellis, such as the original Sugar Snap, to compact bush types like Sugar Ann that stand on their own; older varieties carry a string along the pod that is pulled off before eating, while newer ones are stringless.

our_prose: Sugar snap peas are ready when the pods have plumped up and rounded out, with the peas inside nearly full but the pod still bright green, crisp, and tender, roughly 5 to 8 days after flowering. our_prose: Across the cold northern tier sugar snap peas are a spring crop, with a second fall crop where the season allows. Sow as soon as the ground can be worked, even weeks before the last frost, since pea seedlings are cold-hardy; the spring crop is picked in late spring to early summer and then ends as midsummer heat stops the vines from filling pods and brings on powdery mildew. our_prose: Sweet potatoes are a warm-weather crop grown for the sweet, starchy roots that form underground. Despite the name, they are not related to regular potatoes; they belong to the morning glory family. You do not grow them from seed or from tubers. Instead you plant slips, which are rooted sprouts, set out only after all frost is past and the soil is warm. The plants send out long, trailing vines that cover the ground, so they are grown on ridges or mounds with plenty of room. Sweet potatoes need a long, hot summer (about 3 to 4 months of warm, frost-free weather) and they love heat, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the desert Southwest are the best places to grow them, while cooler northern gardens are a stretch and use black plastic and fast varieties. Go easy on fertilizer, especially nitrogen, or you get lots of vine and few sweet potatoes. Dig the crop before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cure the roots somewhere warm and humid for a week or two, which heals the skins and makes them sweet, and store them warm, around 55 to 60°F. Never put sweet potatoes in the fridge or anywhere cold, which ruins them. This is the opposite of how you store regular potatoes. The young leaves are also good to eat as a cooked green.

our_prose: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a warm-season, frost-tender member of the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae), not a nightshade and unrelated to the ordinary potato despite the shared name. It is grown for its swollen storage roots and planted not from seed or tubers but from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root and set out only after all frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, above about 65°F. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling groundcover, running long vines that root at the nodes, and it is grown on raised ridges or mounds that drain well and give the roots room to expand. The crop needs a long, hot season, roughly 90 to 120 frost-free days, and it relishes the summer heat that stalls many other vegetables, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the low deserts are its stronghold while short-season northern gardens are marginal and lean on black plastic and fast varieties. Feed sparingly and keep nitrogen low, since rich ground grows rampant vine and few roots. The crop is dug before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cured warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F at high humidity for one to two weeks) to heal the skins and turn starch to sugar, and stored warm, near 55 to 60°F. Sweet potatoes are damaged by cold and must never be refrigerated or stored below about 50 to 55°F, the opposite of white potato storage. The young leaves and shoots are also edible as a cooked green.

our_prose: Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris) is a leafy member of the goosefoot family grown for its large, tender leaves and its broad, often vividly colored edible stalks. It is the same species as the beet, selected for leaf and stem rather than root, and it shares the beet's pests, diseases, and multigerm seedball. Its defining trait is an unusual tolerance of both heat and cold: unlike lettuce and spinach, chard does not bolt in summer heat or long days (as a biennial it flowers only after a winter), so a single spring planting crops straight through the summer and well into fall, and in mild zones it overwinters for a harvest that spans much of the year. Harvested cut-and-come-again, the outer leaves picked while the crown keeps producing, one chard plant yields for months. The colorful-stemmed types such as Bright Lights are as ornamental as they are useful, and the stalks cook as a vegetable in their own right.

our_prose: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows turnips on two direct-sown cycles, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah. The spring sowing runs February 15 to March 1, the Group A (Hardy) date for St. George, with roots ready in about 50 days and the crop pulled by late April before the heat builds. USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August, and USU's Group E "Special Plants for Fall Harvest" table does not open the fall turnip window until July 1, so May and June together form a genuine bare-ground pause between the two cycles. The fall sowing runs July 1 to August 1, and USU's fall-gardening guidance for the St. George area specifically groups turnips with carrots and beets as roots that hold well and can be dug quite late into winter, well past the November 1 average first frost.

our_prose: Violas, pansies, and Johnny-jump-ups are cheerful flowers for cool weather. Unlike most flowers, they love the cold: they keep blooming through fall, winter, and early spring in mild areas and bounce back from frost and light snow. What they cannot take is heat. Once summer warmth arrives, they get leggy, pale, and stop flowering well, so in hot areas they are grown as a fall-to-spring flower and replaced when it heats up. The flowers are edible and pretty on a salad or cake, and the little Johnny-jump-up type reseeds itself and pops up on its own year after year.

our_prose: Viola is the classic cool-season bedding flower: garden pansies (Viola x wittrockiana), violas or horned violets (Viola cornuta), and Johnny-jump-ups (Viola tricolor) are short-lived perennials almost always grown as cool-season annuals. They are very frost-hardy, blooming any time the temperature is above freezing and shrugging off light snow, which makes them the workhorse of fall, winter, and early-spring color in mild zones and the first and last color of the season in cold ones. Their one hard limit is heat: blooms fade, stems stretch, and plants turn ragged once sustained warmth above roughly 75 °F arrives, so in most regions they pause or are pulled through summer and return in fall. The flowers are edible, and Johnny-jump-ups self-seed and naturalize.

our_prose: Watermelon is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source as the vines begin to run, and again lightly at flowering. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

our_prose: Yellow summer squash is a warm-season Cucurbita pepo grown, like zucchini, for its tender immature fruit, picked young while the bright yellow skin is still soft and the seeds have not matured. It comes in two forms: crookneck, with a curved, often bumpy neck, and straightneck, smooth and tapered, both sharing the same buttery yellow color and thin edible skin. Plants are bushy rather than vining, fast from seed, and famously productive, so a single plant in good soil can outpace a household at peak. It is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on the same plant, so one plant sets fruit on its own with insect pollination. The two beats that shape a season are pests and pace: squash vine borer and powdery mildew commonly take down a first planting by midsummer, which is why a second sowing pays off, and fruit sizes up so fast that picking every day or two at peak is the difference between tender squash and tough, seedy ones.

our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs yellow summer squash on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah.
